title: The show is finally a hit- but that doesn’t meant it’s perfect #Broad...
transcript: Chess is a musical that has never really fully worked. Pretty much everyone agrees that the score is excellent, but the book has never really worked, despite many, many attempts at fixing it. And while this latest attempt by Danny Strong does its best to keep things moving and cobbled together a coherent plot, it still doesn't quite work and falls into a lot of the Act 2 pitfalls that this show has faced since its inception. However, most people going to chess are not going for the plot. They are going to see these three performers belt their faces off, the standout of which, in my opinion, is Nicholas Christopher. His name will be the least recognizable to general audiences, but he's someone that I've been a fan of for a long time. He was a burr in Hamilton, a Seymour in Little Shop, and probably is most well known for understudying Josh Groban in the recent Sweeney Todd revival. And this is really a star making performance for him. His anthem is, I think, the highlight of the show, and he really does prove that he deserves to be just as big a star as either of the two people on stage with him. Aaron Tveit, I think, is well cast as Freddy the American, and I think this score was a really great fit for his voice. His character is an asshole, which is kind of fun because we've never really seen Aaron Tveit get to play That type of character before Leah Michelle is giving you the classic, buttery smooth Leah Michelle vocals, but unfortunately, I think she is probably the weakest of the three. This is not necessarily her fault, as I think her character is severely underwritten, and I just don't think that this role was a great showcase for her talents in the same way that, like, Fanny Bryce in Funny Girl was. There's also really great supporting performances from Hannah Cruz and Bryce Pinkham. Hannah Cruz is just making an absolute meal of all of the crumbs that she is given, and Bryce Pinkham excels as the enigmatic narrator. Although I did not love all of his quirky one liners, it felt kind of awkward and forced in a way that took me out of the show. This production ultimately feels like a scaled up concert presentation, as the set is incredibly minimal and on par with something that you might see at encores. However, it is elevated by some really stellar lighting by Kevin Adams and some energetic choreography from Lauren Latorre, performed by a really stellar ensemble filled with some of New York's best dancers. So there is definitely a lot to like about this production, and while I don't think it's going to change anyone's mind about chess, it does deliver a really sleek production that I think highlights all of the things that chess does really well, which is primarily its score, and is still a really fun night.
